extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and naturalists / scientists interested in paleontology, archaeology, and atmospheric studies
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and field-method guidance for assessing paleontological/archaeological claims (especially 'fossil man') and for collecting/analyzing atmospheric dust; emphasizes stratigraphic context, sealing, supervised excavation, and microscopic/chemical methods for dust provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary paleontological evidence for evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary and direct evidence in favor of evolution can be furnished only by paleontology: the geological record, when it approaches completeness and is properly questioned, must yield either an affirmative or a negative answer; if evolution took place, there will be its mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether fossil sequences show transitional forms and successive stages linking groups; absence of links may be due to scantiness or imperfection of the geological record, but where the record is sufficiently complete transitions should be evident. Use broad surveys of newly discovered fossil material (e.g., Tertiary mammalia) to test the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional series / successive stages as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of successive stages in fossil series (e.g., civets to hyenas, ancient horse stock to modern horse) provides strong affirmative evidence for evolutionary change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for multiple specimens showing morphological progression across strata; isolated or partial indications are supportive but more complete series strengthen the inference. Use examples and comparisons across deposits to corroborate patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratigraphic association with extinct fauna to establish contemporaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Human bones or artifacts found mingled with bones of extinct Quaternary fauna in gravels, loess, caverns or similar deposits indicate contemporaneity with those extinct species and thus antiquity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the depositional context: presence in Quaternary gravels, cave-earth, or loess; association with land/freshwater fauna (not marine) supports in-situ deposition. Multiple independent lines of sedimentological and faunal association strengthen the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stalagmite (or other speleothem) sealing as proof against intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A floor of stalagmite or other sealing deposit covering and completely sealing underlying beds is both a proof of antiquity and a guarantee that the enclosed contents have not become confused with later objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the stalagmite thickness and superposition relations; use known historic markers (e.g., dated inscriptions partly covered by stalagmite) to constrain deposition rates and minimal ages. If artifacts lie beneath an undisturbed stalagmite floor, intrusion from later times is implausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled, systematic, and supervised excavation procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic explorations carried on without interruption, under competent committees and daily supervision with trustworthy laborers, prevent fraud and confusion of contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain continuous supervision, stratigraphic recording, careful removal of overburden, and trustworthy excavation practices to preclude intermingling of younger and older materials. Detailed records of layers, features, and finds are required to validate claims of antiquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artifact typology as valid evidence of human presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Implements and objects of man's fabrication (stone tools, horn/bone implements) are as good proof of human presence as human bones themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the technology, manufacture marks, and context of artifacts; presence of undoubted human workmanship embedded in sealed older deposits constitutes strong evidence even where human skeletal remains are rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple geological/depositional indicators for antiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine indicators — Quaternary gravels/drift, loess/brick-earth, cave breccia, stalagmite floors, and relation to present river systems — to infer depositional environment and relative chronology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess congruence of sedimentary features with expected depositional processes (glacial/river/loess) and with the faunal assemblage; cross-check regional geomorphology and comparative stratigraphy to support age assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dust-table horizontal collection method
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect atmospheric dust by exposing a horizontal surface of paper (example: two square metres) to the air and sweeping off settled dust with a small brush; the measured weight over a defined period (e.g., 24 hours) represents local fallout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a standardized exposed area for comparability (2 m^2 used by author); record exposure duration and weather conditions; reported yields at Sainte-Marie-du-Mont varied from 2 to 9 milligrammes per 2 m^2 in 24 hours. Preserve samples for microscopic and chemical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rain-water evaporation sediment method for sampling air-dust
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaporate large volumes of rain-water to obtain the sediment representing suspended atmospheric dust; magnetic extraction through this sediment can recover ferruginous particles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect substantial volumes (examples: 100 quarts used) to concentrate trace materials; pass a magnet through the dried sediment to isolate magnetic oxide spherules for subsequent microscopy and chemical testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic and magnetic identification of ferruginous spherules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use microscopy to recognize spherical/melted globules of magnetic oxide of iron in dust, rain-sediment, snow, and on exposed surfaces; extract them with magnets for study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare morphology (spherules, fused globules) with known forms (sparks from flint, aerolite crusts); examine samples from diverse sites (e.g., Notre Dame tower, Mont Blanc snow) to establish ubiquity and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical composition as provenance indicator (meteoric vs anthropogenic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detecting nickel (and cobalt traces) in ferruginous particles indicates a meteoric (cosmic) origin, whereas industrial/metallurgical processes can also produce similar particles and must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform chemical analyses for Ni/Co and compare to known meteoritic signatures; rule out anthropogenic sources by demonstrating occurrence in geological formations predating humans (fossil globules) or by matching microscopical resemblance to aerolite crusts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternative sources and anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for other possible origins of observed particles: volcanic ash, long-range transport of terrestrial sands (diatoms/micro-shells as tracers), industrial emissions, and combusted meteoric material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use biogeographic tracers (diatoms, microscopic shells), historical eruption records, and chemical/mineralogical composition to distinguish sources. Demonstrate that particles occur where industrial origin is impossible (deep geological strata) to strengthen cosmic-origin claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dust explosion risk assessment factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Explosions from suspended dust depend on dust type, particle suspension, presence of combustible gases (e.g., carburetted hydrogen), and specific mixture conditions; certain dusts (starch, coal-dust) can explode under proper conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mixture ratios and available oxygen: example given that 100 cubic metres of air containing ~30 kg oxygen can burn ~27 kg starch-powder or ~11 kg coal-dust. Identify presence of ignition sources and combustible vapors; implement controls accordingly.
